framebox.title: Before we start — what is real and what is not.
framebox.body: The pattern is real: the platform runs live in PROD Switzerland North (app.curavias.ch) with 7 agents serving — advisory-only, never deciding or diagnosing. The hospitals are synthetic and every number you will see is illustrative, on synthetic data with no PHI. To make that realistic rather than invented, we built an Epic core-system simulator that generates all the relevant core-system signals — admissions, transfers and discharges, bed state, OR schedule and staffing — so the agents are driven by the same event patterns a real KIS would emit, without a single patient record. The baseline is real: the synthetic hospitals and the business case are calibrated on published capacity data from four Swiss providers — USZ, LUKS, Klinik Hirslanden and Spital Zollikerberg — alongside federal BFS and cantonal LUSTAT statistics. No confidential provider data was used. The challenges and the people who tested them are real, from dated review sessions with Swiss hospitals.

headings.adapted: What we adapted in the product

challenger.disclaimer: Hospital tenants in the showcase are synthetic (CuraNova · Curalp · Vialta) and all data is synthetic with no PHI. The challengers, their roles and the session dates are real, and each answer is traceable to a dated review report — see

coo.name: Rebekka Hatzung
coo.meta: showcase interview · 24 Jul 2026 · Innovation Hub Zurich
coo.quote: The business case is plausible — but implementations like this fail on IT resources, cost and data quality. And will my people actually use it?
addressed: The metadata-only, deep-link model holds: matching and planning run on metadata, patient data stays in the local KIS and is only referenced. The economics are stated openly — 3-year TCO CHF 5.05M against CHF 11.46M gross benefit, 127% ROI, payback under six months, with a ±30% ROM band and a downside case that still returns 48%.

On adoption we agreed with her, not with the technology: she named data quality and the human factor — acceptance, training, change management — as the real success-or-failure factors. Even experienced staff revert to old ways when overwhelmed. So quality became an agent's job rather than a policy, and the human kept the decision.
value: 127% ROI over three years and payback in under six months — a controlled, ROM-level investment, not an open-ended programme
CHF 11.46M gross benefit against CHF 5.05M TCO — and even the downside case returns 48%
OR utilisation ≥ 85% as the operational target she set in the session
Adoption risk designed out: advisory-only + human-in-the-loop means staff keep authority, so the system is not something done to them
Data quality becomes visible work — gaps get found and routed to an owner instead of quietly discrediting every report
adapted: Data Quality Agent in the runtime — proactive gap detection with owner-routed remediation
Signal triage for controlled onboarding of external golden sources
Change-management & training track written into the offering — technology is not the bottleneck
Polypoint (rostering) documented as a risk path with a fallback; Epic treated as API-first
coo.evidence: Delivery shape validated in session: 2 people / 90 days, main cost being staff effort.

cio.name: Emanuel Furler
cio.meta: challenger question anchoring the field interview · 17 Jul 2026
cio.quote: Welche operativen Entscheidungen könnten heute besser getroffen werden, wenn die zukünftige Kapazitäts- und Auslastungssituation 3 bis 7 Tage im Voraus mit hoher Zuverlässigkeit bekannt wäre?
cio.gloss: Which operational decisions could be made better today if capacity and occupancy were known 3 to 7 days ahead with high reliability?
addressed: Honestly: today Curavias forecasts 72 hours, per ward × horizon-hour, refreshed hourly — that is what is live. Rather than answer from the architecture, we put his question to the clinical front line, and it came back confirmed: the 3–7 day preview was called a major financial and planning advantage, and the agent-based patient flow "fundamentally accurate".

The gap is named, not hidden. Our own North-Star review rates the horizon gap High: operational (72 h) exists, tactical (weekly) and strategic (annual / new-building) do not yet. Longer horizons are a roadmap commitment — stated as such in every review.
value: Pressure becomes visible before it arrives — 72 hours of ward-level foresight, refreshed hourly, instead of discovering it on the morning shift
Decisions move from reactive to planned — the forecast comes with its drivers, so the "why" is arguable
One coordinated plan across beds, OR and staffing rather than three disconnected ones
A validated business hypothesis — the front line, not the vendor, called the preview a major financial and planning advantage
adapted: 72-h occupancy forecast live per ward × horizon-hour with hourly refresh and driver decomposition
Decision Ontology (Sprint 26) — lifts the layer from descriptive to predictive → prescriptive → coordinated
Repositioned from point solution to Integral Capacity Management / Hospital Command Center
Governed decision cadences — daily huddle · weekly tactical · monthly/quarterly strategic
cio.evidence: Horizon extension to 3–7 days is carried as an open roadmap gap (D-02, High) — not claimed as shipped.

cto.name: René Raeber
cto.quote: How do you ensure sovereignty and that the regulatory framework is actually enforced — not just asserted?
addressed: The review corrected a load-bearing assumption: Swiss healthcare regulation is not uniformly enforced at federal level. KVG, nDSG and EPR are national, but implementation and enforcement are delegated to the cantons — and risk ownership ultimately rests with the implementing hospital. Compliance is therefore modelled in two authority layers: national legislative baseline, and cantonal implementation governance, each with its own control mapping.

On sovereignty the recommendation was concrete: the Sovereign Landing Zone — the pattern deployed for Swissmedic — with its four levels from data residency, through global services, to encryption at rest and in use. It is our infrastructure target, with Dev/Test/Prod landing zones already in place.
value: The regulated surface shrinks: with no PHI in scope, data-residency obligations relax substantially — less to defend, less to pay for
Defensible in both directions — a control mapping that answers the canton and the federal baseline, instead of one generic Swiss claim that fails under scrutiny
Reuses a pattern a Swiss regulator already accepted (Swissmedic) rather than inventing a sovereignty story
Risk ownership made explicit — the hospital knows what it carries before signing, not after an audit
adapted: Two-layer compliance model — federal baseline plus cantonal governance, separately mapped
Dual-layer identity — AHV number restricted to authorised roles; capacity processes use internal running numbers; patient linkage only at the endpoint
Capacity-only processing scope — personally identifiable health data deliberately excluded
Dev/Test/Prod landing zones in place, with the Sovereign Landing Zone as the integration target
cto.evidence: Kept open, not closed: secondary re-identification through quasi-identifiers remains a logged design risk.

ciso.name: Daniel von Büren
ciso.meta: AMA Solution Design Review · 10 Jun 2026 · 38 min
ciso.quote: Für eine Bettenplanung brauchst du im Prinzip gar keine Personen- oder Patientendaten … und damit umgehst du eigentlich so ziemlich alles, was rechtlich ein Problem darstellen könnte.
ciso.gloss: For bed planning you fundamentally need no personal or patient data at all — and with that you sidestep just about everything that could be a legal problem.
addressed: He validated the core doctrine and then sharpened it. The Swiss legal rule he named is narrow and clear: data of Swiss patients must not be stored unencrypted outside Switzerland. Cantonal complexity largely dissolves the moment the platform holds no personal data at all — an identifier, a ward, a count, a capacity.

His sharpest challenge was re-identification through small cohorts: pseudonymised data can be reversed when the population is thin — "a 65-year-old in intensive care" may be one of two people. His fix is the one we adopted: reduce to aggregates and counts, and stop there. He also flagged that Entra ID is a global service, so a blanket "Swiss-only" claim needs a documented exception; and raised the Canton-Zurich debate over who ultimately holds the keys — answered with customer-managed keys as a priced, ready mitigation rather than a default.
value: Legal exposure removed at source — there is no patient data to breach, lose or be compelled to hand over
Re-identification made arithmetically impossible, not merely policy-forbidden
A shorter path to approval — the data-protection conversation starts from "no personal data", which is where most of it ends
A priced Plan B means a data-protection objection delays the programme instead of killing it
No residency overclaim to unwind later — global-service exceptions are documented up front
adapted: No-PHI doctrine hardened from a design preference into the security argument itself
Aggregation floor — thin cohorts reduced to counts so re-identification cannot be computed
Identifier translation kept local — re-identification happens in the KIS, never in the platform
Global-service exceptions documented (Entra ID) instead of an unqualified residency claim
Role-based access as the second wall — access follows the role, not the network
Planned break-points ("Sollbruchstellen") — ship simple, keep a priced fallback to run components locally at ≈1.5×
ciso.evidence: His closing verdict: nothing found that was "strange or critical"; on patient-context security, if anything, we had gone further than the case required.

ops.name: Dr. med. Marco Rossi · Christian Ernst · Regula Adams
ops.meta: moderated field interview · 17 Jul 2026 · 60 min · German
ops.quote: How do we get a system that supports us — that gives us back time for patient care and sees what is coming early enough for us to be prepared?
addressed: The real pain point they named was not forecasting in isolation but the coupling of OR utilisation, bed occupancy and staffing — decisions taken in three places that only work when taken together. That is precisely the chain Curavias runs: OOA → BMCA → ORSA → SBA, one coordinated plan across roles, demonstrated live as 102% → 94%.

A second insight reshaped staffing: clinical teams are so specialised that an absence cannot simply be compensated — which makes foresight worth far more than it first appears, and skill-aware staffing mandatory rather than optional. Time for patient care is the promise, and the mechanism is delegation: routine work moves to agents so clinical staff move back to patients — with the human keeping the decision.
value: Time returned to patient care — routine coordination moves to agents, clinical judgement stays with people
One coordinated move instead of three arguments — OR, beds and staffing resolved together: 102% → 94%
Discharge blockers ranked, not listed — 8 candidates reduced to the 5 that are systemic
Specialised absences seen early, when they can still be covered — with "no agency staff" as the goal
Crises rehearsed before they happen — 6 shocks pressure-tested against trusted Swiss signal sources
adapted: Decision Ontology (Sprint 26) — triggered directly by this session: Signal → Understanding → Recommendation → Action → Coordination
Skill-aware staffing (SBA) — specialised roles matched by competency
Ranked discharge blockers (DCA) — systemic blockers surfaced instead of a flat candidate list
Crisis sparring (CSA) — shock scenarios tested against MeteoSwiss, BAG, Alertswiss and SED signals
Metadata-only integration — cloud- and locally-capable, works with Epic without breaching security standards
ops.evidence: Verdict from the front line: the agent-based patient flow is "fundamentally accurate", and the 3–7 day preview a major planning and financial advantage.

it.name: Petrus Jallo
it.quote: How do we establish a governance and cloud target operating model that keeps PID and PHD inside the Swiss regulatory framework — and can prove it?
addressed: This session produced the most uncomfortable correction of the programme: federal Swiss DSG is not automatically the governing basis for cantonal entities. Canton-specific legal mapping is mandatory, and it changes residency, sovereign controls and privacy obligations. A generic Swiss baseline is not enough for a final claim.

The honest position we adopted from it: Curavias is compliance-oriented, not compliance-complete. The operating model aligns strongly on principle — Git-first delivery and infrastructure as code over click-ops, policy-based governance, Zero Trust, environment segmentation, managed identity and RBAC, observability. Evidence linkage is the part still being built, and we say so rather than claiming sign-off readiness.
value: Every control is versioned, reviewable and reversible — governance stops depending on who clicked what
The repository is the audit trail — evidence is a by-product of delivery, not a project after it
Nothing autonomous to defend — AI stays advisory with auditable human decision authority
An honest posture that survives review — compliance-oriented, not compliance-complete, so nothing has to be unwound in front of a regulator
adapted: Git-first delivery and infrastructure as code replacing click-ops — declarative, versioned, rollback-capable
Policy-based governance with Zero Trust orientation and DEV/SIT/PROD segmentation
Managed identity and RBAC as the access model
Observability and auditability built into the platform rather than added for review
Advisory AI with auditable human decision authority carried as a governance requirement, not only a product principle
it.evidence: Named risk we keep visible: architecture maturity running ahead of approved governance creates audit and adoption friction in public-sector settings.
